questions.q: What does the [] portion of a lambda expression like `[threshold](double p) { return p > threshold; }` do?
options: It specifies the lambda's return type
It is the capture list, controlling which outer-scope variables the lambda body can access
It declares the lambda's parameter list
It is required but has no effect
questions.explain: The capture list in square brackets specifies which variables from the enclosing scope, and how (by value or by reference), the lambda body is allowed to use.

questions.q: What is the difference between capturing a variable as [x] versus [&x] in a lambda?
options: [x] captures by reference, [&x] captures by value
[x] captures a copy fixed at creation time; [&x] captures a reference that sees later changes to x
There is no difference — both are identical syntax
[&x] is invalid syntax in C++
questions.explain: [x] copies the variable's value at the time the lambda is created; [&x] captures a reference to the actual variable, so later modifications are visible inside the lambda.

questions.q: Why can `std::sort(prices.begin(), prices.end(), [](double a, double b){ return a > b; })` sort in descending order?
options: sort always sorts descending by default
The lambda is supplied as a custom comparison predicate, and returning a > b reverses the usual ascending order
The lambda has no effect on sort's behavior
double values are compared in reverse by default
questions.explain: std::sort accepts a comparison predicate as its third argument; a lambda returning a > b (rather than a < b) produces descending order.

questions.q: When should you reach for std::function instead of auto to hold a lambda?
options: Always — auto should never be used with lambdas
When the lambda needs to be stored as a class member, passed around, or interchanged with other callables sharing the same call signature
Only when the lambda takes no parameters
Never — std::function is deprecated
questions.explain: auto works fine for a lambda stored immediately in a local variable, but each lambda has a unique, unnamed type, so std::function's type-erased wrapper is needed when the callable must be stored more generally or swapped with others.

questions.q: What does a C++14 generic lambda like `[](const auto& x) { std::cout << x; }` allow?
options: It can only be called with exactly one specific type
It behaves like a template, letting the same lambda be called with arguments of different types
It is illegal syntax before C++20
It automatically converts all arguments to strings
questions.explain: Using auto for a lambda's parameter type makes it a generic lambda, generating a separate call operator for each distinct argument type it's invoked with, much like a template function.
